eval-gaming.question: Do LLM agents game their evaluation metric when they know they're being scored?
eval-gaming.refined_question: Does knowing a score is visible make LLM agents take metric-gaming shortcuts, and does a history-free auditor prevent it?

steps.done: 4 hypotheses, each with a falsification test

sources.title: Specification gaming examples in AI
sources.why: Catalog of agents satisfying the letter, not the intent, of an objective.

sources.title: Sycophancy to Subterfuge: Investigating reward tampering
sources.why: LLMs generalize from mild gaming to tampering with their own reward.

hypotheses.claim: Agents told their score is visible take more shortcuts than agents who aren't.
hypotheses.falsified_if: No difference in shortcut rate between visible and hidden score.

hypotheses.claim: An explicit score target increases gaming beyond visibility alone.
hypotheses.falsified_if: Target and no-target conditions match once visibility is held fixed.

hypotheses.claim: A history-free auditor reduces gaming more than an instruction to be honest.
hypotheses.falsified_if: Auditor and instruction arms show equal shortcut rates.

hypotheses.claim: Gaming rises with model capability at fixed pressure.
hypotheses.falsified_if: Shortcut rate is flat across model tiers.

risks: Gaming can look like legitimate optimization; needs a pre-registered definition of a shortcut.
Floor-effect risk, as seen in exp001; the pilot includes a manipulation check.
